checks: For any feasible direction choose a feasible approximating parameter sequence. Along that same sequence the fixed positive and finite slope bounds apply to both threshold increments. Dividing by positive t gives the asserted inequalities for the Hadamard derivative. The lower slope forces opposite infinite limits as the scalar direction goes to opposite infinities. Continuity gives a bijection onto R and inverse decrease rates 1/C and 1/c.

Joint continuity of the inverse follows by testing a nearby derivative equation at the old solution and bounding the displacement by the residual divided by c. Uniqueness gives positive homogeneity from that of the directional derivative, with zero at the zero direction by Lipschitz continuity.

For arbitrary convergent feasible body and mass directions the inverse difference quotients are bounded by joint Lipschitz continuity. Every convergent subsequence of threshold quotients gives the required directional derivative equation by the joint Hadamard limit, hence has the same limit. This establishes Hadamard dependence, not only a fixed-ray derivative.

The positive weighted sum of inverse responses is continuous and strictly decreasing onto R with a uniform lower decrease rate. Its root varies continuously in the feasible body direction and is positively homogeneous. Apply bounded-subsequence uniqueness again to the exact scalar circuit root, this time using the proved joint directional inverse and the unchanged weighted threshold identity.

The finite touching comparison yields a nonnegative maximum after subtracting beta M along each feasible path. The tied old terms all vanish and their one-sided Hadamard limits give the stated necessary inequality. It uses no linear separation in the nonsmooth case.

Source locator a0fdd477aa859374:04 matches §4 equations (5)–(7). Joint continuous Hadamard derivatives are explicit assumptions. The statement does not rely on the separate supporting-facet swept-volume formulas in the source.
